metaDescription: Multi-tier terraced retaining walls for steep London, Ontario backyards, turning unusable slope into level, usable outdoor space. Free quotes.
h1: Terraced Retaining Walls in London, Ontario
intro: Some London backyards, particularly ones backing onto the Thames River valley, have too much grade change for a single wall to handle safely or affordably. Terracing splits that grade into level, usable steps instead.

sections.heading: When One Wall Isn't the Right Answer

blocks.text: A single wall tall enough to retain an eight or ten foot slope requires significant engineering, deep excavation and a large budget. Splitting that same grade change into two or three shorter, properly set-back walls is often safer, less expensive, and creates usable level space at each tier.
This comes up often on London's steeper river valley lots, where a homeowner wants a patio or garden level partway up the slope, not just a wall holding the whole hill back at once.

items.title: Grade survey
items.text: We map the full slope to determine how many tiers make sense and where each wall sits.

items.title: Setback spacing
items.text: Each upper wall is set back from the one below by a distance based on wall height, so the lower wall isn't carrying the upper wall's load.

items.title: Individual drainage
items.text: Each tier gets its own weeping tile and drainage stone, not a single system for the whole slope.

items.title: Construction in sequence
items.text: Lower walls are built and backfilled before upper walls begin, in the correct engineering order.

blocks.text: An upper terrace wall built too close to the wall below it adds surcharge load the lower wall wasn't designed for. Proper setback is what makes terracing work structurally, not just visually.
The City of London treats each wall's height individually for permit purposes, but a terraced system as a whole is usually reviewed together. We manage permits and engineering across the full design.

Turning an unusable slope into two or three level, landscaped areas tends to add more functional living space to a London property than a single retaining wall alone, which is part of why terracing is popular on river valley lots.
See /retaining-walls-and-property-value for how a well-executed grade solution factors into overall property value.
Steps or a sloped path connecting each terrace level are part of the design conversation from the start, so the finished result is functional to move through, not just visually tiered.

faqs.q: Is terracing more expensive than one tall wall?
faqs.a: Often less expensive overall, since shorter walls need less engineering and reinforcement per section, even though there are multiple walls.

faqs.q: Can I put a patio or garden on one of the terrace levels?
faqs.a: Yes, that's one of the main advantages, each tier creates level, usable space rather than one continuous slope.

faqs.q: How many tiers does a typical London slope need?
faqs.a: It depends on total grade change and desired tier height, usually determined during the site survey. Most residential terracing uses two or three tiers.

faqs.q: Do all the tiers need their own drainage?
faqs.a: Yes, each wall in a terraced system gets its own weeping tile and drainage stone rather than sharing one system.

faqs.q: Does terracing add more value than a single retaining wall?
faqs.a: It can, since terracing typically creates more usable outdoor space than one wall holding back the same total grade change.

faqs.q: Are steps included in a terraced wall design?
faqs.a: Yes, we plan steps or a connecting path as part of the overall design so each level is actually usable, not just visually separated.
